title: The Crossing
body: Humans come ashore on Dia-thìr, bringing their Church with them, and are given leave to stay. They are the first strangers met since the Sundering.

title: The ships met off the north-west
body: That winter the mist that had lain on the western sea since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it lifts. Two fishing boats of Achadh àrsaidh, working the water off the north-west cape where the Sea-Watcher is seen, meet three ships coming out of the thin grey from the west, and hail them; neither side understands the other. The fishers turn south and the ships follow them down the coast toward Cuan shean. The fishers call the place Coinneachadh nan Long, the meeting of the ships, and the boats of Achadh àrsaidh still slow there.

title: Three ships off Cuan shean
body: Three ships out of the west anchor off Cuan shean, the first hulls of their size seen from Dia-thìr since the fleet of the Sundering. Their master, a captain the rolls name Edmund Harrow, comes ashore unarmed with eleven men and asks by signs for water.

title: Forty days on the dunes
body: The custodians of Cuan shean will not decide alone, and send inland to the capital for counsel. For forty days the strangers are fed on the beach and kept below the dunes.

title: The custodian of Baile fhiadhaich rides south
body: Word of the ships reaches Baile fhiadhaich, up the western coast, in three days. Its custodian rides south to see them, and writes to the council that the strangers' ropes are better than ours and their manners worse.

title: The Council of Custodians grants leave
body: The Council of Custodians at Cathair dhearg, which has sat in the crown's place since the crown fell empty at the close of the Age of Sundering, confirms the strangers' leave to stay under the high custodian Tormod mac Ailein. The council roll gives the vote as with one voice; a later hand in the margin notes that three custodians were absent.

title: The quarter of sea they came from
body: Old sailors at Cuan shean say that the strangers came in from the same quarter of sea the fleet of the Sundering sailed into. The council forbids the saying in its hall. It is written down all the same, and never answered.

title: The land beyond
body: The strangers name their homeland in their own tongue, but no scribe of the Dia-thìrich writes the word down. From the first season the scribes call it an Tìr Thall, the land beyond, and its people simply the humans.

title: The first attempts at speech
body: For a whole season clerics of the humans' Church and custodians of Dia-thìr labour to make a store of words in common. Neither side's account of what was agreed survives whole.

title: Wren's word-lists
body: The human cleric Samuel Wren and the custodian Gormshuil nic Fhearchair keep word-lists side by side through the season of speech-making. Wren's list survives in the Administration's letter-books. Gormshuil's is lost; only its first leaf, with forty words for the colours of broken coal, is known from a copy.

title: One word for the coal
body: The humans have a single word for the coloured coal, and it is their word for the black fuel they burn at home. Gormshuil's copyist notes that no Dia-thìris word in either list answers to it, and that the humans did not ask for one.

title: Trade begins
body: At first the trade is fair on both sides: the goods of Dia-thìr for tools and knowledge the lonely island lacks. For a few years it seems it may last.

title: The trading post at Ros dhomhain
body: The humans set up a trading post at Ros dhomhain, the capital's harbour, and give iron tools, window glass, lamp-oil and paper for wool, salt fish, hides and dyed cloth. The first tally-book of the post, kept by the trader Thomas Pike, balances evenly through its first year.

title: The first hull on Loch chrom
body: Pilots of Caol leathan bring the first of the strangers' ships up the Abhainn gheal into Loch chrom, towing her with boats through the shallows below Baile ghlas, and she anchors off Ros dhomhain. Thereafter the humans' goods come to the capital shore by water, and the pilots charge a stranger's hull twice the toll of a Dia-thìreach boat.

title: Cathair naomh sends its wool
body: Cathair naomh, the city above Seann Toll on the northern coast, sends its first wool south to the humans' post by coasting boat. Its custodians take their payment in paper and ink, and with them begin the town's roll afresh.

title: Iron in the smithies
body: The smiths of Cathair dhearg take the humans' bar-iron gladly and learn to temper it in a winter. Within a few seasons the old bronze hoes are melted down for bells.

title: Dyes for Baile Mòr mhòr
body: The weavers of Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast trade their cloth for the humans' dyes, a red and a blue brighter than any the island could make. Within a few years the old madder fields about the town go back to grass.

title: Harrow's second voyage
body: Harrow sails west with hides and dyed cloth and comes back with four ships in place of three. He brings carpenters, a surgeon, and a letter from a trading house in an Tìr Thall asking what else the island has.

title: The shipwrights of Inis mhòr
body: The shipwrights of Inis mhòr come to look at the humans' hulls and measure them with knotted cords. Their guild had built nothing greater than a coaster since the fleet of the Sundering, and the old craft of building for deep water was half forgotten.

title: The surgeon Jonas Tull
body: The humans' surgeon, Jonas Tull, sets the broken leg of a fisherman of Cuan shean who had been given up as lame. The town's custodian enters it in the roll as the first debt owed to a stranger.

title: Salt from Seann Warr
body: The salt-pans of Seann Warr begin to sell to Pike's post by the barrel. They are the first goods of Dia-thìr that the humans come back asking for twice.

title: Wool at Caol leathan
body: The walled harbour of Caol leathan sends its first wool-ship to the humans' post. Its merchants will be paid only in iron by weight, and the tally-book of the post names them the hardest bargainers on the island.

title: The first mixed settlement
body: A small coastal town takes in both Dia-thìrich and humans under one rule. It is not tried again.

title: Baile dhìreach under one council
body: The small port of Baile dhìreach on the south-west coast takes Dia-thìrich and humans under one council of six, three of each. Its founding compact is written twice, once in each tongue, the only such compact of the age.

title: The first council of Baile dhìreach
body: The council is chaired in alternate years by the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim and the human carpenter William Rook. The harbour dues go half to the custodians at Cathair dhearg and half to the humans' post.

title: Inis thais declines the compact
body: The city of Inis thais, whose harbour lies a few miles from Baile dhìreach, is bidden to join the joint council and declines. Its custodian writes that one town may be a trial, but two would be a rule.

title: A supply ship lost on the western reefs
body: A human supply ship strikes the reefs off the western coast in fog, and nine of her crew drown. Her master was sailing by a chart drawn from memory, the humans' letter-books complain, on a coast lit only by the old driftwood fires.

title: The beacons asked for
body: Human seamen, strange to the coasts of Dia-thìr, ask for standing beacons. The builders of the Dia-thìrich agree, not yet seeing what the beacons will bring.

title: The beacon headlands walked
body: The human navigator James Fenn and the Dia-thìreach mason Torcall Clachair walk the coast together to choose the places of the new beacons, and mark the five headlands of the old fires. Fenn's chart survives; Torcall's cairns for the most part do not.

title: Fenn's line
body: On the same survey James Fenn runs a line of sights across the whole island, from the open sea off the north-west, where ships from the west first raise the land, to the water off the eastern cape. He makes it two hundred and twenty-one miles, some forty-five of them sea at the western end. It is the first measure of Dia-thìr from side to side, and every chart the Company draws afterwards is scaled to it.

title: A marriage in two tongues
body: At Baile dhìreach the net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh weds the human cooper Samuel Hale. The council enters the marriage in both its books; the custodians at Cathair dhearg, asked for a ruling, send none.

title: The first written treaty
body: The terms on which the humans stay are first set down in writing, in the humans' tongue only. No one among the Dia-thìrich speaks against it at the time.

title: The treaty signed at Cathair dhearg
body: The treaty is signed in the council hall at Cathair dhearg by Tormod mac Ailein for the custodians, and for the Administration by Josiah Pell, newly come as the humans' first Commissioner. Tormod could not read the tongue it was written in. Who read it to him is not told.

title: The Residency above Ros dhomhain
body: Josiah Pell builds a house of dressed stone on the rise above Ros dhomhain and calls it the Residency. Captain Harrow, needed ashore no longer, goes back to the sea trade.

title: The Company chartered
body: Harrow and Pike found a trading house under licence of the Administration, known on Dia-thìr simply as the Company. Its charter gives it first refusal of "all fuels, ores and minerals the island may yield."

title: The warehouse at Cathair dhomhain
body: The Company builds a stone warehouse at Cathair dhomhain, along the lake shore from the capital, to keep its tools from the harbour thieves of Ros dhomhain. It is the first building on Dia-thìr the Company owns outright.

title: The strangers' fever
body: A fever comes ashore at Cuan shean with a crowded ship and runs down the west coast. Ninety-one Dia-thìrich die, and eleven humans. The custodians shut the town to ships for a season, and Pell protests in writing.

title: The fever at Baile àrsaidh
body: The strangers' fever comes to Baile àrsaidh, a day's walk up the coast, and kills its custodian and both her sons. No humans dwell in the town at all, and the custodians of the west take note of it.

title: The fever turned back at Cnoc àrsaidh
body: At Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west the townsfolk block the road with carts and turn back every traveller for a season, and the fever does not reach them. The Administration fines the town for hindering trade.

title: Prospectors in the central hills
body: The Company sends two prospectors, Abel Stone and Hugh Mercer, into the hills east of the capital. They come back with sacks of broken coal, and word that the black seam runs "further than can be walked in a day."

title: The sacks returned to the rock
body: The custodians of the vein demand the broken coal back, to lay it in the rock again with the proper words. The Company returns half. The custodians' roll enters the other half as "carried west."

title: The first mining contracts
body: Trade sours into bargain. Dia-thìrich hands mine the vein on a scale that no reverent custom had ever used.

title: The first pit at Muileann chrom
body: Under the first contract a Dia-thìreach crew of thirty opens a working at Muileann chrom, paid by the ton in iron tools and lamp-oil. The custodians' own cuttings had never been measured by weight at all.

title: A coal quay at Ceann fhada
body: The Company builds a stone quay at Ceann fhada, a fishing hamlet below the hills, for loading coal into coasting barges. The fishermen are paid for their foreshore in iron nails, by weight.

title: Wren's grammar
body: Samuel Wren finishes a grammar of Dia-thìris for the Mission, the house of the humans' Church on Dia-thìr. It is careful and true in most things, and it gives the word for the vein's custodians as "keepers of the coal."

title: The hawk-priests read Wren
body: The hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag ask the Mission for a copy of Wren's grammar, to read what the humans write of them. The Mission sends one. Of all the copies that survive it bears the most notes in the margins.

title: The Mission chapel
body: The Mission raises a timber chapel on the quay at Ros dhomhain, the first church on the island. Its bell is the first iron bell on the island, and the custodians ask that it not be rung before the fishing fleet is out.

title: The first refusal
body: One mining settlement will not sign a contract. For the present it is passed by, not punished.

title: Beathag Dhubh of Doire mhòr
body: The settlement that refused was Doire mhòr, in the hills above Muileann chrom, and its custodian was Beathag Dhubh. Her answer to the Company's agent is known only in his words: that the hill was not hers to sell nor his to buy.

title: The road around Doire mhòr
body: The Company opens its next working at Cnoc fhiadhaich instead, and runs its cart-road round the fields of Doire mhòr and not through them.

title: Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg lit
body: The first of the new beacons is finished on the southern headland at Tobar dhearg: a round tower of grey stone raised over the old fire-tower, paid for by the Company, with a Dia-thìreach keeper. Torcall Clachair builds it; James Fenn sets its lens.

title: The first keeper of Tobar dhearg
body: The first keeper of the southern beacon is Anna nic Dhòmhnaill of Tobar dhearg village, a fisherman's widow, who climbs the tower twice a night for the rest of her life. The village holds the keepership as a trust and keeps it in its own families through the age.

title: Raiders in the north-western waters
body: A Company brig is boarded off the north-west coast and stripped of her cargo of tools. The raiders are never known. The Administration blames the custodians of the coast, and the custodians answer that those waters have always kept their own law.

title: The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
body: Samuel Wren copies the writing on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag and sends it west to the scholars of an Tìr Thall. No answer comes. The custodians tell him the stone is older than the Dia-thìrich and that none living can read it.

title: The first coin
body: The humans' coin is brought in beside the old barter, for ease, it is said. Within ten years nothing that needs a tool from over the sea can be had for anything else.

title: The mark and its hundred pence
body: The coins are struck at Ros dhomhain from silver and copper shipped from an Tìr Thall: the mark and its hundred pence. The first striking bears a ship on one face, and nothing of Dia-thìr on either.

title: Cathair mhòr refuses the mark
body: The market of Cathair mhòr, greatest below the hills east of the capital, refuses the humans' coin for a whole year. The custodians of the town give way when the Company's tool-sellers will not cross their bridge.

title: Two books at the capital market
body: At the market of Cathair dhearg the tool-sellers take only marks, while cloth and fish still go by barter. The custodians' clerks begin to keep two sets of books, and complain of it in both.

title: Wren's winter at Dùn thais
body: The masters of the druid school at Dùn thais receive Samuel Wren for a winter of disputation. He asks them why the vein should be holy; they ask him why his fuel should be burned. Neither telling of that winter names a winner.

title: Drochaid Cathair dhearg rebuilt
body: Company masons rebuild in dressed stone the old bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg, wide enough for coal-carts to pass two abreast.

title: The Commissioner's carriage
body: Company wheelwrights build a closed carriage for Josiah Pell, and he drives in it over the new bridge from the Residency to the council at Cathair dhearg. It is the first carriage on the island. The custodians still walk to the council, and say so.

title: The Harbour Articles
body: A second compact, the Harbour Articles, fixes the dues and anchorages of Ros dhomhain in the Company's favour. Like the first treaty it is written in the humans' tongue only, and this time two custodians refuse to sign.

title: The fishermen of Baile ghlas
body: The fishermen of Baile ghlas, whose boats had anchored free at Ros dhomhain time out of mind, are charged anchorage under the Harbour Articles. They take their catch to their own small harbour and sell it there to anyone but the Company.

title: The northern concession
body: The council grants the Administration upland pasture in the north-west about Muileann àrsaidh, for human families who will not work in the pits. The grant is for grazing; the families build houses of stone.

title: Death of Tormod mac Ailein
body: Tormod mac Ailein, the high custodian who signed the first treaty, dies at Cathair dhearg. The council chooses Coinneach Glas of Ceann àrsaidh after him, who had never met a human before the Crossing and has dealt with little else since.

title: Harrow lost at sea
body: Edmund Harrow's ship does not come back from the western crossing. The Company passes wholly into Thomas Pike's hands, and the humans' letter-books mourn Harrow as the man who found Dia-thìr.

title: The Small-Burning Law lapses
body: Centuries of measured burning end within one generation. The Law is never repealed; once its keeping no longer pays, it is no longer kept.

title: The last count at Doire mhin
body: The custodians of Doire mhin keep the old count of the Small-Burning Law, the measure of coal that might be burned in a year, one season longer than any others. They enter it in their roll with the note that no one asked for it.

title: A defence of the Law at Dùn dhearg
body: Fionnghal nic Artair, a custodian of Dùn dhearg, writes to the council in defence of the Small-Burning Law, the only such defence that survives. She holds that the Law was never for the coal's sake but for the people, who would become whatever the burning made them.

title: Murchadh Seabhag preaches at Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell the hawk-priest Murchadh Seabhag preaches that Mòd, the Hungry Hawk of Acaill, starves those who eat faster than the land can feed them. The sermon is copied and carried to the camps, and it is the first writing of the Dia-thìrich that the Company's agents are told to seize.

title: The hearths of Achadh naomh
body: The households of Achadh naomh, in the hills north of the workings, who keep Na Seann Spioradan, will not light their hearths with coal bought of the Company. They burn peat as their grandparents did, and their elders teach that coal burned for wages is burned without the ancestors' leave.

title: Burning by the cartload
body: The Company's furnaces at Muileann chrom burn coal by the cartload to drive the new pumps, and no heed is paid to the custodians' tally of what the hill may give in a year. Coinneach Glas's council asks that the tally be kept, and is sent a copy of the Company's accounts.

title: Henry Maddox Commissioner
body: Josiah Pell sails home to an Tìr Thall and does not return. After him comes Henry Maddox, bidden to double the yield, with a letter from the Company promising him a share of it.

title: The oaks of Cathair fhada
body: Maddox buys the oak woods about Cathair fhada for pit-props. The town had cut them sparingly for generations; they are gone within the working lives of the men who fell them.

title: The first deaths of haste
body: A tunnel worked faster than any Dia-thìreach crew would have worked it falls in and kills eleven. It is entered as an accident.

title: The eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich
body: The fall was at Cnoc fhiadhaich, in a gallery driven forward without the timbering the Dia-thìrich crews had asked for. The custodians' roll names all eleven dead. The Company's report names none, and calls the gallery "unsound ground."

title: The coughing sickness
body: A dry cough runs through the camps at Muileann chrom and Cnoc fhiadhaich, worst among the boys who break coal at the pit-mouth, and thirty-eight die of it. The Mission's surgeon calls it a winter complaint. It lasts through the summer.

title: The orphans of Cill thais
body: The village of Cill thais takes in the children orphaned by the coughing sickness and keeps a house for them at its own custodians' cost. The Company, asked to give toward it, sends a crate of Mission primers.

title: Taigh-solais Baile ìseal lit
body: The second beacon is lit on the eastern shore at Baile ìseal. Torcall Clachair, now too old to climb, directs its building from a chair at the foot of the headland.

title: The keepers of Baile ìseal
body: The keepers of the eastern beacon are drawn from the fishing families of Baile ìseal. The town's custodians ask for a rule, and get it, that the lamp be lowered on the nights the boats go out to the deep grounds, lest the fish take fright. When the rule lapsed no one wrote down.

title: Seòlaid Ceann òg
body: The traders' boats from the new quay at Ceann òg go down the Abhainn ìseal past Cnoc bheag and Inis bhàn to the north coast, west along it, round the western capes, and south past Inis thais into the capital's water. Their lane is called Seòlaid Ceann òg after the quay. Off the north-west it swings far out into the open sea, and there the ships bound for an Tìr Thall leave it and the ships from the west come in.

title: The camp at Àth ìseal
body: The Company builds a camp of timber huts at Àth ìseal, at the ford below the new workings, for crews brought in from the coast. It is the first settlement on Dia-thìr made for nothing but the pit.

title: Doire mhòr's water taken
body: The Company turns the stream that watered Doire mhòr to wash coal at Cnoc fhiadhaich. No order is written; the stream is dammed one season and not let go. Beathag Dhubh's people carry water by hand for two summers, and then begin to leave.

title: The short hunger in the hills
body: The men drawn from the farms into the pits, the hill villages of Muileann chrom lose their oats to rain, with none at home to cut ahead of it. The Company sells meal at the camp stores for marks, and the villages have few.

title: Meal-carts at Doire fhiadhaich
body: The villages of Doire fhiadhaich in the south send carts of meal north to the hill villages, as the old custom of the Holy Age bids in a hungry year. The Company's agents at Àth ìseal buy up two of the carts on the road.

title: The mountain dug by the ton
body: For the first time in the history of Dia-thìr the mountain is worked by the ton, and for ends no custom of the Dia-thìrich would have chosen.

title: Rope for the winding-gear
body: The rope-walks of Dùn chrom, which had made cable for the fishing boats, turn wholly to winding-rope for the pit-heads. The Company pays well, and the town grows by half.

title: The Company's second charter
body: The Company is chartered again in an Tìr Thall, with new money and a new name the Dia-thìrich never take up. Its agents at Ros dhomhain now outnumber the Administration's own clerks four to one.

title: Barges at Cidhe Beag
body: Coal barges begin to load at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine and float the black coal down to the coast. The old canoe landing, used since before the Sundering, is widened with cut stone, and its shrine is moved uphill.

title: Abhainn uaine silts black
body: The washing of coal upstream fills Abhainn uaine with black slurry, and within a few seasons the salmon runs at its mouth fail. The river keeps its name, the green river, and the fishermen speak it bitterly.

title: Baile Mòr dhomhain a barge town
body: As the coal comes down to it from Cidhe Beag, Baile Mòr dhomhain on the river road grows into the busiest barge town of the north. Its people double in number, most of the newcomers bargemen from the coast.

title: Baile dhomhain raised as a camp town
body: A Company surveyor lays out a second camp, Baile dhomhain, on a grid, the first town of the Dia-thìrich drawn on paper before it was built. Within two seasons it houses four hundred.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr reopens
body: The old carters' house at the half-way stage of the coal road between the capital and the hills is built again, opens its doors at Lùnastal, and keeps the name An Taigh-seinnse Mòr. Its first keeper, Seònaid Bhàn, takes both marks and barter, the only innkeeper on the road who will.

title: Rathad na Mèinne
body: The Company's road-gangs finish metalling the carriers' road from Cathair dhearg by Doire chaol and the ford of Àth chiar to the workings at Achadh dhomhain, wide enough for coal-carts to pass both ways. The carters call it Rathad na Mèinne, the mine road. The posts with the crown's sign that had marked it since the Age of Sundering are left standing along it.

title: The carters of Doire chaol
body: The carters of Doire chaol, on the road just east of the capital, band together in a guild to bargain with the Company over the rates for hauling coal. It is the first Dia-thìreach guild of the age, and the Company owns it because that is cheaper than breaking it.

title: Seann Toll made a coal landing
body: The Company takes the river landing at Seann Toll, below the workings, and builds a loading stage there for the barges that carry the coal down the Abhainn uaine to Ceann leathan. The town's fishing boats are moved to the next reach.

title: The coal ships' lane
body: From the landing at Seann Toll the coal barges go down the Abhainn uaine to Ceann leathan, where the Company's ships load at the river mouth and go out by the southern lane, Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, west along the south coast to the wild strait and the open sea. The fishers of the south coast, who had used the lane for five hundred years, learn to keep out of the coal ships' way.

title: The first Dia-thìreach overseer
body: A Dia-thìreach is set over other Dia-thìrich miners, answerable to human masters. It is the first open crack within the Dia-thìrich themselves, and not only between them and the humans.

title: Raghnall Maor
body: The first overseer is Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill of Muileann chrom, a crew-leader who had worked the pits since the first contract. He is given the Company's staff and a house with a slate roof, and from the office the Dia-thìrich give him his byname: Raghnall Maor, Raghnall the steward.

title: The overseers multiply
body: Within a few years there are overseers at every working in the district, all Dia-thìrich, all answerable to the Company's agents. The custodians' roll no longer names them, and gives only their number.

title: Seumas Dubh killed at Cnoc mhòr
body: Seumas Dubh, overseer of the new pits at Cnoc mhòr, is killed by his own crew after a boy is crushed on a haulage he had ordered hurried. The Company hangs two men at Ros dhomhain, the first hanging done by the Administration on Dia-thìr.

title: Hawk-priests barred from the camps
body: Henry Maddox bars the priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig from the camps, for their preaching slows the work. The overseers enforce the order, though several of them are hawk-faithful, as the roll says. The Mission's chaplains, who keep a chapel in every camp, are not barred.

title: The pox at Ros dhomhain
body: A spotted pox comes ashore at Ros dhomhain on a Company ship and climbs the coal road into the camps. The Mission counts four hundred and six dead. The custodians count more, and write the difference in the margin of the Mission's list.

title: The pox in the south
body: The pox spreads south from the harbour to Baile chiar and the villages about it. The custodians there cut the names of the dead into the stone lintel of the council house, and they can still be read.

title: Baile dhìreach loses its harbour dues
body: The Administration moves its customs house from Baile dhìreach to Ros dhomhain and ends the sharing of the harbour dues. The mixed council, left with half an income, cuts its members from six to four.

title: Arthur Lisle Commissioner
body: Henry Maddox leaves Dia-thìr a rich man. Arthur Lisle, a lawyer, comes after him, and his first act is to have every compact since the first treaty copied into one bound book.

title: A customs house at Ros gheal
body: Lisle opens a second customs house at Ros gheal on the northern coast, where hawk-faithful fishing towns had traded with Company ships without paying dues. The customs officer is twice chased out of the town in his first year.

title: The silver of Muileann chiar
body: The humans seek to claim the silver seam at Muileann chiar as well. It is one of the few things the Dia-thìrich keep wholly in their own hands through all this age.

title: Ùna nic Choinnich and the silver guild
body: The silver seam was held for the town by its guild of refiners, led by Ùna nic Choinnich. When the Company's surveyors came she met them at the adit with every member of the guild and all its ledgers, and bade them find the humans' name anywhere in either.

title: The Silver Compact
body: Arthur Lisle, reading the treaties closely, finds nothing in them touching silver. On Là Fhèill Brìde he signs a compact with the silver guild leaving the seam to the town, the first writing of the age in which the Dia-thìrich keep the better terms.

title: Seann Bhral the silver port
body: The silver guild sends its bars to the sea by the old port of Seann Bhral and not by the Company's quays, and pays the port's custodians in silver for the use of it. The Company finds no ground in the compact to object.

title: The carters of Baile gheal
body: The carters of Baile gheal in the south-west take up the carrying of Seann Warr brine-salt round the lake to the capital, a trade the Company does not trouble to claim. It keeps the town's folk out of the pits for the whole age.

title: Taigh-solais Àth dhearg lit
body: The third beacon is lit on the north-east coast at Àth dhearg. Its keeper, Tormod mac Pheadair, keeps a daybook of every ship he sees, and from his book the number of human sailings in these years is known.

title: Àth dhearg builds the tower
body: The masons of the beacon at Àth dhearg are its own townsmen, paid half in marks and half in the promise that the tower will guide their own boats home. Tormod mac Pheadair, the keeper, is one of them.

title: Pirates off the eastern coast
body: Raiders in low black boats take a Company coal ship off the eastern coast and burn her to the waterline, cargo and all. The Company says the silver guild paid them. The silver guild says nothing.

title: A cove burned near Ceann leathan
body: A Company gunboat hunts the raiders to a cove near Ceann leathan and burns every boat drawn up on the shingle, most of them belonging to the town's fishermen. The raiders are not found.

title: The end of the joint council
body: The mixed council of Baile dhìreach breaks up in a quarrel over a boundary wall and never meets again. The human families go to Ros bheag and Ros dhomhain; the Dia-thìrich families stay. Households that were both split or fell silent, and which did which is not told.

title: The boatyard moves to Inis chrom
body: The human boatbuilders of Baile dhìreach move their yard to Inis chrom, a day's sail east, where the Company has promised them timber. The town takes them in without a joint council or any other compact, and within a generation they fade from its rolls.

title: The dry year in the east
body: For a single season the rain fails over the eastern farmlands about Achadh shean. It is remembered after as a warning no one heeded, for the next drought, long after, came three years together.

title: Baile ruadh loses its seed
body: At Baile ruadh in the east the drought kills the seed corn in the ground, and the town borrows seed from the Company's store at Seann Dunn, at a price paid back over five harvests. It is the first Dia-thìreach town to owe the Company a debt in grain.

title: Aonghas mac Coinnich's question
body: At Dùn thais the druid master Aonghas mac Coinnich puts to his students a question the school's register calls new: why the humans cannot see the colour in broken coal that every Dia-thìreach child sees. He does not answer it, and the register notes that he called it the wrong question.

title: The druid students of Baile Mòr uaine
body: Students of Aonghas mac Coinnich carry his question to Baile Mòr uaine and teach it in the town's hall of disputation. The hall's record of the argument runs to four hundred leaves, and ends, like his, without an answer.

title: Cathair gheal in the northern concession
body: The human families of the northern concession found a market town at Cathair gheal, with a stone hall for their magistrate and a chapel. The Administration issues its charter without asking the custodians.

title: Human farms at Cnoc ghorm
body: Human farmers of the concession clear land beside the Dia-thìrich village of Cnoc ghorm in the upland north-west, and build a mill. The villagers sell them grain until the mill is working, and then stop.

title: A fishing station at Ceann mhòr
body: A few human fishing families of the concession settle at Ceann mhòr, the harbour under the north-western headland. They are the first humans to fish the island's waters for a living and not for the Company's table.

title: The first Dia-thìreach child sent over the sea
body: One family, hoping for better treatment, sends a son to be schooled in the humans' homeland. He is never known to return.

title: The family of Eachann Mòr
body: The family that sent its son away was that of Eachann Mòr, a custodian of Ceann àrsaidh who had lost his seat on the council. The boy, Calum, sailed west on a Company ship with a letter from the Mission and a purse of marks.

title: The Mission school
body: The Mission opens a school at Ros dhomhain for Dia-thìrich children, taught in the humans' tongue. It takes thirty pupils in its first year, most of them overseers' children, and among them the Mission counts its first Dia-thìrich converts.

title: Schooling at Inis bhàn
body: The custodians of Inis bhàn in the north open a school of their own in answer to the Mission's, and teach the old reckoning, the rolls and the names of the hills. The Mission complains that the pupils come to its school the next year already knowing how to argue.

title: Tobacco on the concession farms
body: Human farmers of the northern concession plant tobacco on the sheltered slopes behind Ceann mhòr and sell the dried leaf to the Company's ships. Of the crops the humans brought, it alone is still grown on Dia-thìr.

title: Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: The Company rebuilds the old bridge over the river at Ros fhionn to carry the eastern coal road. While the carts run it is the busiest crossing on that side of the island.

title: Coal through Inis bheag
body: Coal from the eastern workings is carted over the new bridge and down to the river quays of Inis bheag, and goes by barge to Caol chrom at the river mouth for shipping. The Company deepens the river at the quays, and the town's old fish market is moved to make room for the coal stage.

title: Baile mhin ships the eastern coal
body: The river quays of Baile mhin, below Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag, take the eastern coal that Inis bheag cannot load. The townsfolk are paid by the barge, and with the gain the town builds its first stone houses.

title: Caol gharbh passed by
body: The coal road to Inis bheag passes Caol gharbh by a mile, and the town, which had hoped for the traffic, gets only its dust. Its custodians write that they had not known a town could be harmed by a road it was not on.

title: The thing in the north-western sea
body: The crew of a Company brig see a beast greater than their ship off the north-western headlands. The Administration's clerk files their report with the complaints about pirates, and the Dia-thìrich sailors of the coast say they had wondered when the humans would see it.

title: A brig lost in the mist
body: A Company brig bound for the northern landing with tools is caught by a gale in sea mist off Eilean fhada and driven onto the skerries. Her crew wade ashore at low water and walk to the harbour at Caol bheag. Thereafter the Company's charts mark the northern passage closed to its ships from midwinter to the end of spring, the season of the gales.

title: Whale-boats out of Àth fhionn
body: Human fishermen of the concession teach the boats of Àth fhionn to hunt whales with the hand-lance, and not wait for them to strand. The oil is sold to the Company for its lamps, and from this time whale-boats go out from the north coast every summer.

title: Surveyors lost at Doire uaine
body: Two Company surveyors go up into the hills at Doire uaine against the villagers' counsel and are not seen again. The Company sends a search party, which comes back after a day and will go no further.

title: The offerings at Doire uaine
body: After the surveyors are lost the villagers of Doire uaine leave salt and coal for the sìth at the foot of the hills, as their grandparents did after any death on the high ground. The Company forbids coal to be left lying and has the offerings gathered up, and the villagers leave salt alone.

title: The tithe raised
body: The share of mined coal taken by the humans' Administration rises steeply. What the Dia-thìrich receive does not rise with it.

title: Lisle's tithe schedule
body: The new schedule goes out from the Residency under Arthur Lisle's hand and raises the Administration's share from one part in five to one part in three. The custodians receive a copy in the humans' tongue, with a rendering made by a Mission pupil.

title: Weighing the grain at Dùn fhiadhaich
body: At Dùn fhiadhaich the tithe-gatherers begin to weigh grain as well as coal, saying the town's farms feed the pits and share in their gain. The custodians' roll calls it the tithe on the tithe.

title: The flux at Ros dhomhain
body: A bloody flux breaks out in the crowded quarters at the Ros dhomhain quays. The Mission's nurse, Anne Colby, makes a sick-house of the chapel, and it is said that she kept the dead below two hundred.

title: The flux reaches Seann Vell
body: The coal barges carry the flux to Seann Vell, the river port east of the capital on the Abhainn fhionn. The custodians of the town shut the barge landing for a season, and the Company fines them for it.

title: Walter Crane Commissioner
body: Arthur Lisle dies at the Residency of a fever of the heart. Walter Crane, who had been the Company's chief agent at the pits, is made Commissioner after him, the first to hold both offices one after the other.

title: The pay office at Ceann mhin
body: Crane moves the Company's pay office for the southern workings to Ceann mhin, and makes the crews walk there to be paid, a day each way, in place of sending the paymaster to them. The crews are not paid for the walk.

title: Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor
body: Raghnall Maor dies, and the Company gives his staff to his son Dòmhnall. The overseer's office, which the custodians had hoped would die with the man, becomes a family's inheritance.

title: Taigh-solais Muileann bheag lit
body: The fourth beacon is lit on the northern shore at Muileann bheag, the first to burn coal and not oil. Its keepers say the flame throws a colour on the water that no oil lamp ever did.

title: The fishermen of Muileann bheag
body: The fishermen of Muileann bheag complain that the colour the coal flame casts on the water drives the herring off. The keepers do not change the lamp. Within a season the herring come back, and the complaint is withdrawn in a letter the Company keeps.

title: The dig at Làrach an Teampaill
body: The Mission cleric Edwin Lowe digs for a season at Làrach an Teampaill with Company labourers, seeking proof of an older faith on the island. He finds cut stone, burnt bone and marks he cannot read, and writes that the ruin's builders "were not the present race." The custodians agree, and add nothing.

title: The pillar at Cnoc chiar
body: Edwin Lowe copies the writing on the pillar near Cnoc chiar and sets it beside Wren's copy of the obelisk at Cnoc bheag. He judges that the two scripts are not the same, and that neither is of the Dia-thìrich. His notes stop there.

title: The column at Cnoc ghorm
body: Lowe's last copy is of the column near Cnoc ghorm, and beside it he writes that its marks are like the pillar's, but not near enough to help. He leaves Dia-thìr the next year and takes his notebooks with him.

title: The glass-house at Baile Mòr dhìreach
body: Peter Voss, a glazier left behind when his Company contract ended, builds a glass-house at Baile Mòr dhìreach and melts the white sand of Cuan ruadh with charcoal from the hills. It is the first glass made on Dia-thìr. Within a generation his Dia-thìrich apprentices carry the craft to the towns of the capital shore.

title: The silver guild refuses again
body: Martha Gale, an agent of the Company, offers the silver guild of Muileann chiar a partnership, on terms the guild's ledger calls generous. Ùna nic Choinnich, now very old, has the offer read aloud twice in the guild hall, and it is refused by show of hands.

title: The camp at Achadh dhomhain
body: A new camp is opened at Achadh dhomhain for the deep galleries under the hill, and within a few seasons it is the most crowded place in the district. Its houses are built of spoil.

title: Cloth for the camps at Dùn chiar
body: The weavers of Dùn chiar take a Company contract for canvas for the camp tents and sacks for the coal, and the town thrives on it. Its custodians note that never before had the town made anything for a use it did not approve.

title: The first of the undying generation
body: A girl is born in the mining camps who takes more raw coal into her body over her life than any Dia-thìreach in living memory, and she does not age as the folk about her age. Her name is Aisling.

title: The coach to the camps
body: The Company puts a coach on the road between the quay at Ros dhomhain and the camps at Muileann chrom, twice a week each way, changing horses at the old waypoint houses. Clerks and overseers ride in it. The crews walk.

title: The coal weighed at the quay
body: The Company sets up a great steelyard at the Ros dhomhain quay, and thenceforth the island's yield is known by the ton and the hundredweight. The custodians' old count, kept in seasons of labour, is no longer entered in the roll.

title: Ros dhìreach the second coal port
body: The Company opens a second coal stage at Ros dhìreach on the southern coast for the workings south of the hills. Its first cargo is lost in a squall off the harbour mouth, and the fishermen moved to make room for the stage will not go out after it.

title: The nameless change
body: What is befalling the child born two years before has as yet no name in any tongue spoken on the island. Decades pass before anyone tries to make one.

title: The first steamer
body: The first ship driven by an engine comes into Ros dhomhain, a Company paddle-steamer out of an Tìr Thall. The fishermen row out to look at a ship going against the wind with no sail set. Within a generation the Company's coal goes out in nothing else.

title: The shrine at Cill dhìreach
body: At Cill dhìreach, a village at the edge of the workings, the custodians keep a small shrine where the pit crews leave the first piece of coal from each new gallery. The Company suffers the custom, for it costs a stone a gallery.

title: The keepers of Cill ghlas
body: The custodians of the shrine at Cill ghlas, in the hills among the workings, keep the old rites at the mouth of the oldest cutting while the Company's pits deepen about them. It is the last shrine in the district that the pit crews still visit on the old feast days.

title: A' Phlàigh Uaine
body: The Green Death goes through the mining camps. The coal dust is blamed, though no study of it is ever finished. Twenty-six settlements have cases.

title: The first cases at Achadh dhomhain
body: The Green Death is first marked at Achadh dhomhain: a greenish pallor, then a cough that brings up dark dust, then weakness. The camp buries forty in the first month, in a field beyond the spoil-heaps still called the green acre.

title: Twenty-six settlements
body: The sickness spreads along the coal roads from the camps at Muileann chrom, Àth ìseal and Cnoc fhiadhaich, and falls hardest on Ros dhìreach, Ceann òg, Inis ìseal, Baile dhomhain, Achadh fhada, Cnoc bheag, Muileann uaine, Cuan àrsaidh and Inis bhàn. The custodians' roll lists the twenty-six settlements that had cases, and leaves a blank line after the last, as though waiting for another.

title: The Green Death at Baile chrom
body: The Green Death comes to Baile chrom in the hills, not the town of that name in the north-west. The scribes keep the two apart with care, for in later tellings of the island's hungers they are confused.

title: Àth ghlas burns its huts
body: At Àth ghlas the custodians order every hut where a death has been burned with its bedding. The Company protests the loss of its property. The custodians note that the sickness stops sooner at Àth ghlas than anywhere else.

title: The dead of Cnoc naomh
body: At Cnoc naomh the dead of the Green Death are laid in the burial ground of the town's old shrine until it is full, and then in a field outside. The field is never ploughed again.

title: Doctor Bright's study
body: Nathaniel Bright, physician to the Administration, begins to study the sickness at Muileann chrom, weighing the dust in the lungs of the dead. In the second season of the work he falls ill, and his notebooks break off in the middle of a table.

title: Walter Crane dies of the Green Death
body: Commissioner Crane, who had walked the camps in the worst of the sickness, dies of it at the Residency. Martha Gale, the Company's agent at Ros dhomhain, holds his seal for the months until another comes.

title: George Tolley Commissioner
body: George Tolley comes from an Tìr Thall with orders that the yield must not fall for the sickness. He does not visit the camps. His letter-book blames the dust, the Dia-thìrich custom of sleeping near the fire, and the custodians' shrines, in that order.

title: Quarantine at Caol mhin
body: Tolley sets a quarantine station at Caol mhin on the northern coast for ships from an Tìr Thall, and holds them offshore until their crews are looked over. It is the first order of his rule the Dia-thìrich approve, and they say so.

title: The camps turn to the hawk
body: The hawk-priests still barred from the camps, the crews carry their sermons in themselves. The overseers' reports of these years list hawk-feathers nailed above hut doors as a matter for punishment.

title: Anne Colby's sick-houses
body: Anne Colby opens sick-houses at Àth ìseal and Achadh dhomhain and nurses there until the sickness ebbs. She is the only human the camp folk name in their own accounts of the plague, and they name her kindly.

title: The huts of Cnoc gharbh
body: After the sickness the people of Cnoc gharbh, who had worked the southern galleries, leave their camp huts and go back to the old village on the hill. The next year the Company builds the huts again and brings in crews from the west.

title: The first strike
body: A whole mining settlement stops work for eleven days over conditions worsened by the plague two years before. The strike ends when the food, which the humans' Administration holds, runs out.

title: The strike at Baile thais
body: The settlement was Baile thais, below Cill ghlas, and the crew-leader Catrìona nic Eachainn called the halt after the Company would not close the galleries where the Green Death had been worst. For eleven days no coal left the town. On the twelfth the Company's store, the only store, was empty.

title: The Company's granary
body: After the strike the Company builds a granary of its own at Muileann chrom and forbids the camps to keep grain beyond a week's ration. The overseers enforce the order, and Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor signs it.

title: Fish smuggled from Ros gharbh
body: The fishermen of Ros gharbh carry salt fish up to the camps by night, past the Company's granary rule. The custodians' roll calls it the only trade of that decade that ran the right way.

title: Catrìona goes to the silver town
body: Turned out of Baile thais and refused work at every Company pit, Catrìona nic Eachainn goes east to Muileann chiar, and the silver guild takes her on as a refiner. The Company asks that she be sent back. The guild's answer was filed and has not survived.

title: The springs at Muileann ruadh
body: The Administration builds a new bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh for its officers mending from fevers. Dia-thìrich who had bathed there for centuries are let in on certain days, and charged a penny.

title: Muileann chiar grows
body: The silver town grows beside the coal workings, for the humans want both, and the digging goes faster than the old reverence would ever have allowed.

title: A second Muileann chiar
body: The silver trade crowds the old town, and the guild settles its refiners and carters in the coal-breakers' mill town to the west, which is called by the silver town's name from then on. The rolls call them the old town and the new, and do not always say which they mean.

title: Silver for marks
body: The silver guild begins to sell bar silver to the Company for marks, at a price the guild sets. It is the only ware on Dia-thìr in this age priced by Dia-thìrich hands, and the guild's hall fills with human coin.

title: Silversmiths at Muileann bhàn
body: Silversmiths settle at Muileann bhàn on the road to the silver town and live by working the guild's bar into ornaments for the humans' market. Theirs is the one Dia-thìreach craft sold in an Tìr Thall under a Dia-thìreach name.

title: Macha's priests bless the coin
body: At Tolley's asking the priests of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg, the order of the capital and the crown, bless the Residency's new coin. The priesthood of Macha teaches that the two horses of her rite, Dubh Sainglenn the black and Liath Macha the grey, each have their due; the dissenting priests say the coin is only one of them.

title: The second change of coin
body: The barter goods of the Dia-thìrich are marked down against the humans' coin a second time, on terms the humans' Administration alone sets.

title: Wool marked down at Baile Mòr fhionn
body: At Baile Mòr fhionn, where wool had been the measure of every bargain, a fleece is now worth by the Residency's table what a half-fleece was worth before. The town's weavers stop bringing wool to market and send it over the sea on their own account, until the Company refuses them freight.

title: The boats of Caol fhiadhaich sold
body: The fishing fleet of Caol fhiadhaich, unable to pay the new harbour dues in marks, sells half its boats to the Company. The men who sailed them go into the pits under the next year's contracts.

title: The dissenters go to Cnoc bheag
body: Priests of Macha who refused the blessing leave the capital's temple and settle in the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag. There they keep the older reading of Macha's two horses, and take in custodians who have lost their seats.

title: Iain Maor
body: Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor dies, and his son Iain takes the overseer's staff. Iain Maor is the first overseer schooled at the Mission; he keeps his reports in the humans' tongue and his household in Dia-thìris.

title: The Levy
body: Tolley issues an ordinance, the Levy, by which every farming village in the west and north must send one in five of its able grown folk to the pits for two years. The villages are paid in marks, at the new rate.

title: Levy officers at Caol mhòr
body: The Levy's officers take their first tally at Caol mhòr in the north-west, reading the names of the chosen from a list in the humans' tongue. The custodians of the town write the names again in Dia-thìris, that they may know whom to look for.

title: The Levy in the north-west
body: The Levy falls hardest on the villages about Baile chrom and the northern concession, which had never sent crews to the pits. The Dia-thìrich of the concession are taken; its human farmers are spared.

title: Baile ìseal sends its people
body: Baile ìseal sends forty-one of its people to the pits under the Levy, and nineteen come back when their term ends. The custodians' roll names the other twenty-two and the camps they were sent to.

title: Muileann naomh buys its way out
body: The custodians of Muileann naomh pay the Levy's officers in silver to halve the town's tally. The officers take the silver and the whole tally. The complaint is lodged at the Residency and filed.

title: The druid school's hall shut
body: George Tolley shuts the hall of the druid school at Dùn thais over a lecture on whether the humans' blindness to the coal's colour is a kind of sickness. The masters go on teaching in their own houses, to smaller rooms each year.

title: The last disputation at Doire chiar
body: At Doire chiar, a village of the druid schools north of the eastern workings, the masters hold the last open disputation of the school on the eve of Bealltainn, in the open air on the village threshing-floor. Its matter is whether a question may be forbidden. The Administration's clerk who attends writes that it may.

title: Teaching in the sacred forest
body: Druid masters who may no longer teach in a hall begin to teach under the trees in the sacred forest of Flidais near Muileann chiar, where the Administration has no building to shut.

title: Building the last beacon at Baile chrom
body: Work begins on the fifth and last beacon, on the north-western headland at Baile chrom, with masons taken by the Levy from the very villages whose fields they leave untilled.

title: The masons of Cnoc thais
body: The Levy takes the masons of Cnoc thais to build the beacon at Baile chrom. Their foreman, Dùghall Clachair, cuts the names of his crew into the lintel of the lamp-room, the only writing on any of the five towers.

title: The five beacons complete
body: The ring of coast beacons is finished: Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Baile ìseal, Muileann bheag, Àth dhearg and Tobar dhearg. They serve a trade that is by now plunder in all but name.

title: Cuan ruadh loses its trade
body: The ring of beacons finished, the Company's steamers round the island without putting in, and within a few years the old coasting trade of Cuan ruadh up and down the eastern shore dies.

title: Taigh-solais Baile chrom lit
body: The beacon at Baile chrom is lit with a coal flame, and the ring is whole. The Company's ships can now round the island by night, and the keepers' daybooks show the sailings doubled within a few years.

title: Gorta Baile chrom
body: The Great Hunger follows a failed harvest across thirty-four settlements, made worse because the Levy has taken so many to the pits that too few are left to till the land.

title: Baile chrom goes hungry
body: The hunger is worst at Baile chrom itself, whose people could see the new beacon from their empty fields. The custodians write that more died there than anywhere else, and the Administration, which kept its own count, does not gainsay them.

title: The famine country
body: The custodians' roll draws the bounds of the famine country along the north-west shore and the hills behind it. Within them lie Baile chrom in its own shire; Ceann mhòr, Àth fhionn and Àth dhearg in the shire of Ceann mhòr; Muileann àrsaidh in the shire of Cnoc thais; and Achadh àrsaidh in the shire of Muileann àrsaidh. Thirty-four settlements are counted within the line, and the roll gives the dead of each.

title: The hunger at Doire ghlas
body: At Doire ghlas in the north the hunger takes the old and the very young first. The village sends its young folk to the camps for the Company's rations, and by the year's end it is half empty.

title: Inis mhin eats its seed
body: In the second winter of the hunger the townsfolk of Inis mhin on the north coast eat their seed corn. The Mission kitchen at the harbour feeds three hundred a day for a season.

title: The hunger reaches Seann Bhrenn
body: The hunger reaches as far east as Seann Bhrenn, where the custodians open the old grain-pits of the Holy Age, unfilled in living memory. They hold only dust.

title: The relief ship
body: A relief ship with grain from an Tìr Thall lies a month at Ros dhomhain while the Residency and the Company dispute who shall pay for its unloading. Meanwhile the Mission opens kitchens at Cathair gheal and Baile chrom, and Anne Colby, come back to the island, keeps the one at Baile chrom.

title: The Levy set aside
body: The Levy is set aside in the famine districts, too late for the harvest. It is not repealed. The custodians note that it was never used again, nor needed to be, for the villages had learned what it meant.

title: Cnoc mhòr walks south
body: Rather than starve, the families of Cnoc mhòr in the north walk south to the camps and take work under the Company. Their village stands empty for a generation.

title: Robert Haskins Commissioner
body: George Tolley retires with honours. Robert Haskins, who follows him, orders that the custodians' council be consulted on the tithe, and then sets the tithe before the council has met.

title: Customs at Seann Dunn
body: Haskins opens a customs house at Seann Dunn on the eastern coast, and a Company store with it. The store sells the east its seed and its tools, and within a few years its ledgers hold the debts of half the district.

title: The first petition
body: For the first time the custodians of the Dia-thìrich act together, and not settlement by settlement, and lay a written grievance before the humans' Administration. It is not answered.

title: The gathering at Ceann àrsaidh
body: The petition was drawn up at Ceann àrsaidh by custodians of nineteen settlements, meeting for the first time as one body. Peigi Ghlas, custodian of Cill ghlas, carried it to the Residency and handed it to a clerk.

title: Àth fhionn signs
body: Ruairidh mac Thormoid, custodian of Àth fhionn in the south-east, is the eldest of those who signed the petition. He was born before the humans' coin was struck, and says so beside his name.

title: Grievance first written
body: From these years come the oldest writings of grievance among the Dia-thìrich that survive. No hand is yet raised in them; yet in them it is first written that something has gone wrong.

title: Leabhar Baile thais
body: The oldest of them is a book of complaints kept at Baile thais, set down by many hands over some years: wages, deaths, the granary, the stream at Doire mhòr. The custodians' copyists call it Leabhar Baile thais.

title: The songs of Fearchar Bàrd
body: The poet Fearchar Bàrd, a breaker of coal at Muileann dhearg since boyhood, makes songs of the Levy and the famine, and they are sung in the camps. The overseers forbid them, and because they were forbidden several were written down.

title: Songs at An Taigh-òsta Grianach
body: The songs of Fearchar Bàrd are sung in the roadside houses of the east, and An Taigh-òsta Grianach becomes known for them. The Company's carters sing them too, the keeper writes, not always knowing what they sing.

title: The Company's deep-water quay
body: The Company builds at Ros dhomhain a deep-water quay for the new iron steamships, which burn the island's own coal to carry it away. Fearchar Bàrd makes a song of that, the most quoted of all his songs.

title: The deep quay at Ceann chaol
body: A second deep-water quay is built at Ceann chaol in the south-east for the eastern coal. Its builders are brought from the coast, and the village of forty houses becomes a town of four hundred.

title: Baile thais walls its pithead
body: The Company rings the pithead at Baile thais with a stone wall and a gate, and pays a watchman to count who goes in. It is the first working on Dia-thìr walled against its own crews.

title: Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at the silver town
body: Catrìona nic Eachainn dies at Muileann chiar, a refiner of the silver guild to the end. The camp folk of Baile thais send men to her burying, and the Company docks each of them a day's pay.

title: The quay fire
body: A fire starts in the Company's coal sheds at Ros dhomhain and burns three days, taking two streets of the harbour quarter with it. The Company's inquiry finds no cause; the harbour quarter's own account has several.

title: The council without a high custodian
body: After the death of the last high custodian the Council of Custodians cannot agree on another, and sits for years with the seat empty. Robert Haskins writes to an Tìr Thall that this makes the council easier to deal with.

title: Tiormachd Achadh shean
body: The Long Drought lies on the island's dry season three years together, and bears hard on a people already worn thin by the tallies of the pits.

title: The wells of Achadh shean
body: At Achadh shean, whose name the drought bears, the wells fail in the second summer, and the cattle are driven west in a column the roll calls a day long. Fewer than half reach water.

title: The dry country
body: The custodians' roll counts ten districts of the east as drought country, worst at Achadh shean, Àth uaine, Achadh àrsaidh and Muileann chiar, and reaching down to Cuan ruadh and west toward Baile chaol. The Administration keeps no count of its own.

title: The cattle of Baile chaol
body: At Baile chaol the herds are slaughtered in the second summer of the drought, rather than watched as they die. The salt meat is sold to the Company for the camps, at a price the Company names.

title: Doire fhionn walks for water
body: At Doire fhionn in the east the women walk each day to the spring at Àth ruadh and back for water, half a day's journey. The custodians record it for the three dry years, and then cease.

title: Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
body: The spring of Allt an Àigh, said never to have failed, runs on through all three dry years. Pilgrims who keep Na Seann Spioradan come to it from all the east, the first of them at Bealltainn, and the Administration sets a watchman to charge them for the water. He is called back after one season.

title: The pilgrims' road at Inis uaine
body: Pilgrims bound for Allt an Àigh gather at Inis uaine, and the townsfolk feed them freely, as the Old Spirits require. The town's own wells are low, and it gives away more water than it keeps.

title: Drought-fever at Baile Mòr ruadh
body: A fever of foul water follows the drought into the towns, worst at Baile Mòr ruadh, where the wells had been deepened into the old middens. Two hundred and sixty die. The Mission's report is the first to name the cause rightly.

title: The fever at Cnoc shean
body: The drought-fever spreads to Cnoc shean, whose one well is found tainted. The custodians close it, and for a year the town drinks from carts.

title: The Mission's wells
body: The Mission sinks deep wells at Achadh shean and Àth chrom with a boring-rig brought from an Tìr Thall, and they hold. The custodians of the east set down the Mission's wells and the Company's tallies on facing pages, without comment.

title: Achadh chaol goes to the pits
body: Their fields burned out by the drought, the people of Achadh chaol in the north-east go to the pits for wages, the first villagers of the eastern farm country to do so. Their custodian writes it down as the end of the village, not a flitting.

title: The tally not lowered
body: The coal tally is not lowered in the drought. The custodians of the east, their joint petition unanswered, each write to Haskins alone; to each he answers that the matter is under consideration.

title: The petition of Àth mhòr
body: Iseabail nic Leòid, custodian of Àth mhòr, writes the longest of the single petitions, forty pages listing her town's dead beasts. Haskins answers in two lines. Both survive, bound together by a later clerk.

title: The first inheritance of mixed blood
body: A suit over whether the grandchild of a marriage between a Dia-thìreach and a human may inherit the customary rights of mining is decided, and the Administration makes the ruling wholly to its own gain.

title: The case of Thomas Hale
body: The child was Thomas Hale, grandson of the marriage at Baile dhìreach of Eilidh nic Ruairidh and Samuel Hale, who claimed a share in a customary cutting through his Dia-thìrich grandmother. Oliver Dunstan, magistrate at Ros dhomhain, ruled that customary rights descend only through the line the Administration owns, and that it owns only its own.

title: Dunstan's rule applied
body: Within a few years Dunstan's ruling is used to pass eleven customary cuttings to the Company, each because some holder in the line had married a human or been born of one. The custodians stop entering such marriages in the roll.

title: A cutting at Cnoc dhubh taken
body: Among the cuttings taken under Dunstan's rule is the old customary working at Cnoc dhubh, held by one family since the Holy Age. A great-grandmother of the line had married a human sailor; that is enough.

title: The Lamp-Watch
body: A fellowship of pit crews calling itself the Lamp-Watch begins to meet at Baile thais and Cnoc chaol under cover of a burial club. Its first known deed is to pay for the burying of an old breaker who had died in the Company's lock-up.

title: Edward Vane Commissioner
body: Robert Haskins is called home after a quarrel with the Company over the price of steamship berths, and Edward Vane follows him. Vane is the first Commissioner born on Dia-thìr, at the Residency, and he speaks Dia-thìris, badly, but he speaks it.

title: The tram-road to Ros dhìreach
body: Vane lays an iron tram-road, drawn by mules, from the southern workings down to the coal port at Ros dhìreach. It halves the cost of shipping coal, and ends the carting trade of the villages on the old road.

title: The night-shift order
body: For the first time the digging is made to run without ceasing, day and night, and the mountain is given no season of rest at all.

title: The night crews at Cnoc chaol
body: The order falls first on Cnoc chaol, where the Company's newest galleries are opened to crews working by coal-lamp in two shifts. The custodians' roll writes that the hill was given no silence at all, and leaves the rest of the page blank.

title: The night-shift strike
body: The crews at Cnoc chaol refuse the night shift, and within a week are replaced by crews brought from the coast under the Company's new contracts. The Lamp-Watch keeps the strikers' families for a season, and then its money is gone.

title: The strikebreakers of Muileann dhomhain
body: The crews that replace the strikers at Cnoc chaol are brought through Muileann dhomhain, where the townsfolk turn them from every door. They sleep in the Company's barns, and several go home the next season.

title: Matthew Dunne's sermon
body: Matthew Dunne, the Mission's minister at Ros dhomhain, preaches against the night-shift order from the chapel pulpit, saying the Dia-thìrich are right that even the ground must rest. The Company complains to the Mission, and Dunne is called back to an Tìr Thall. The Lamp-Watch copies the sermon and reads it in the camps.

title: The lung-rot at Cnoc chaol
body: A wasting sickness of the lungs spreads among the night crews at Cnoc chaol and Baile thais. Unlike the Green Death it kills slowly. The Company pays the widows a pension for a year, then stops.

title: Iain Maor and the night shift
body: Iain Maor, overseer at Muileann chrom, writes to the Company that the night shift is killing his crews faster than it is paying for them. The letter survives because the Company filed it with his dismissal, which was undone a month later for want of anyone else.

title: The coal line
body: The Company opens its railway from the pits at Muileann chrom down by Cathair dhearg to the deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain. Its engines burn the island's own coal, as the steamships do, and the tram-road to Ros dhìreach is left to the mules. Within a year the carters' guild of Doire chaol, which had hauled the coal on Rathad na Mèinne for eighty years, loses the long haul. From the first day the Dia-thìrich call the engine carbad-iarainn, the iron chariot, and the railway the coal line.

title: Coal-lamps from Baile ghorm
body: The potteries of Baile ghorm take a contract for clay lamp-bodies for the night crews, thousands in a year. The potters' own book notes that they are the first lamps made on the island for work in the dark by command.

title: Fionnan born
body: A second child is born bound to the coal as Aisling was, half a century after her. So it is known that the thing is no chance of one birth: it comes of the digging, and it will go on.

title: The Administration's count of the people
body: The Administration counts the people of Dia-thìr by district for the first time. Its figures for the humans are true to the household; for the Dia-thìrich they are rounded to the hundred, and in the hill districts to the thousand.

title: The district of the outer coasts
body: The Administration makes the outer coasts one district and rules it from the harbour office at Seann Vell on Eilean ruadh, where its revenue cutters lie: the islands of the west and south, Eilean bhàn with Cuan dhearg and Cnoc chaol, and the southern edge of the windy coast in the far north-west. Its surveyors walk to the edge of the great moss there, which no chain can cross, and go no farther. Beyond it the district map is left blank.

title: Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, last of the druid masters
body: Seònaid nic Dhùghaill, the last master of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean to teach openly in this age, dies at Dùn thais. No one is named after her, and the school's register ends with her death. It is taken up again only long after the humans are gone.

title: The custodians' rolls at Muileann chaol
body: The custodians of the east begin to send copies of their rolls for safe keeping to the town of Muileann chaol, which still kept Beathag nic Thòmais's loft of papers, beyond the Residency's reach. The copying is done in the houses of three families, and the copies kept in a cellar.

title: The second Muileann chaol
body: Some of the copies bound for Muileann chaol go by mistake to the smaller town of that name further north, and are kept there for years before the mistake is found. The custodians note that they were kept just as well.

title: The word found at last
body: With two children now known, the custodians agree on a word for what is befalling them: fuil-ghuail, "coal-blood", rendered in the humans' tongue as coal-touched. It is meant as a physician's word. It outlives that meaning.

title: The custodians who named it
body: The word was agreed at a meeting of custodians at the shrine of Cill ghlas, where the oldest cutting still stood open. They chose a plain word, fit for the physician's book. The roll gives the vote; who first put the word forward it does not say.

title: The Line of Aisling found
body: Cailean mac Eachainn, a copyist in the cellar at Muileann chaol, finds in the roll of the camp at Àth ìseal the marriage of Aisling's father, Donnchadh mac Thormoid, with his line written seven names back, as the custodians write a marriage. He carries the seven names up to Tobar dhìreach, to Ealasaid of Clann na Ceiste, the last who says the lines, and she knows them for the line of Somhairle son of Ailean Mòr. She says Aisling's line to him backward, from her father to the mason who found the fire. So what the camps whispered at Aisling's birth is found to be true. Cailean writes the line in the margin beside her birth.

title: The Administration's register
body: The Residency, hearing of the word, orders that any Dia-thìreach child showing the change be reported to the Commissioner's office. The custodians obey by reporting none.

title: The third change of coin
body: The old barter of the Dia-thìrich is struck down as lawful payment altogether. Every bargain on the island now goes by the humans' coin.

title: The barter houses closed
body: The barter houses at Ros dhomhain and Cathair dhearg, where cloth and fish had changed hands without coin since before the Crossing, are shut by order. A clerk of the Residency writes that the ledgers are now "complete for the first time."

title: The fishwives of Inis mhòr
body: The fishwives of Inis mhòr, who had sold by barter at the river steps since before the Crossing, will take no coin for a week, in protest at the shutting of the barter houses, and give their fish away. The Company's clerks record it as a glut.

title: Marks borrowed at interest
body: Barter being struck down, the hill villages borrow marks at interest from the Company's stores to buy seed. Within a few years most of the villages of Muileann chrom owe the Company more than a year's crops.

title: The old market at Muileann òg
body: The old barter market at Muileann òg, where hill and coast had met to trade since the Holy Age, closes after its last season. The ground stands empty until, long after, it is used for a fair.

title: Mòrag nic Iain Maor
body: Iain Maor dies, and his daughter Mòrag takes the overseer's staff at Muileann chrom, the first woman to hold it. The Company approves her in a letter that calls her "a safe pair of hands."

title: Charles Merriman Commissioner
body: Edward Vane dies at the Residency. Charles Merriman comes after him with a small company of armed constables, the first standing force the Administration has kept on Dia-thìr.

title: The constable post at Muileann shean
body: Merriman's first constable post is built at Muileann shean on the northern coal road, a stone house with a yard for horses. The townsfolk call it the humans' second Residency, and do not mean it kindly.

title: A barracks at Tobar ghorm
body: A second post is raised at Tobar ghorm, near the northern workings. The village's custodian is paid rent for the ground, and with it buys the village out of its debts to the Company store.

title: A grey-night vigil at Baile chrom
body: The Mission at Cathair gheal reports that human labourers near Baile chrom keep vigil by night in the fields, praying in silence under the sign of a grey goose, which they call the wild goose of the Spirit. The Mission cannot find whence the practice came, and calls it irregular, a superstition learned of the Dia-thìrich. The Dia-thìrich of Baile chrom disown it.

title: Manannan's priests on the grey night
body: The priests of Òrd Mhanannain at Ceann mhòr answer the Mission's report of the grey-night vigils. The practice owes something to the Dia-thìrich, they say, but to their own harbours and not to Baile chrom: the human fishing families of Ceann mhòr learned from them the night prayer to keep the sea shut, and the labourers inland keep it as a vigil of their Church, a night of silence under the wild goose of the Spirit in place of a prayer to Manannan. The priests call it Manannan's prayer gone astray, and do not admit its keepers to their house.

title: The dockers' strike at Ros dhomhain
body: The dockers of Ros dhomhain, Dia-thìrich and human alike, refuse to load coal for nine days over the new berth charges. It is the only strike of the age in which human workers stand with Dia-thìrich. Merriman's constables break it, and the human dockers are shipped west.

title: Seann Vell's dockers stay out
body: The dockers of Seann Vell, the harbour next to Ros dhomhain, refuse to load the coal sent to them during the strike. When it ends they are not shipped west, for there are no humans among them; but they are not hired again either.

title: Lorccan born
body: A third such child is born, in a mining town and not a camp; the thing is no longer bound to any one place.

title: Cian born
body: A fourth is born within a year of the third. Never again do the children of the undying generation come so close together.

title: Blasting-powder at Cill ghlas
body: The Company begins to drive galleries under the hills about Cill ghlas with blasting-powder shipped from an Tìr Thall. The custodians of the shrine ask that no charge be set within sight of the old cutting. The Company's engineer marks their asking on his plan, and sets the charges below it.

title: Powder landed at Caol ìseal
body: The blasting-powder for the new galleries is landed at Caol ìseal on the northern coast, away from the crowded southern harbours, and carted inland under guard. The town's custodians ask what is in the barrels and are told it is lamp-oil.

title: Scàineadh Cill ghlas
body: The Rending: in the hills east of the capital, about Cill ghlas, the earth tears open along a fault beneath a common working. Dozens are killed, and a whole mining district is shut for a generation.

title: The first open fight
body: A mining death, which the Dia-thìrich workers lay at the door of the humans' carelessness, leads to the first bloodshed between the two peoples.

title: The shrine at Cill ghlas lost
body: The Rending swallows the old cutting at Cill ghlas, where the custodians had kept the rites through all the age, and its shrine with it. The custodians' roll sets down the loss of the shrine before the loss of the dead; a later copyist has put them in the other order.

title: The district closed
body: The Company shuts the whole district of the Rending and fences it, leaving Cill ghlas, Àth chaol and their hamlets in the shires of Muileann dhearg and Muileann chiar without work. The villages empty toward Baile thais and Muileann dhearg, and the closed district is left to the thorn.

title: The meeting on the moor road
body: The folk turned out of the closed district send their eldest to the custodians of Muileann dhomhain, who meet them at a standing stone on the moor road below the town, lest the Company's clerks see them in the town hall. At the stone the custodians lend them the land at the edge of the fenced ground. The place is called Coinneachadh an Fhearainn, the meeting of the land.

title: Achadh chaol raised by the dispossessed
body: Folk of the closed district build a new village at Achadh chaol, at the edge of the fenced ground, on land lent by the custodians of Muileann dhomhain. It is the only settlement of the age founded by Dia-thìrich for Dia-thìrich with no Company surveyor's hand in it.

title: The fight at Muileann chrom
body: The death that began it was a flooded gallery at Muileann chrom, where seven died after the pumps were stopped to save fuel. When the Company's agent came to the pithead the crews stoned him and his constables, and the constables fired. Four Dia-thìrich and one constable were killed.

title: Mòrag Maor at the inquiry
body: At the Administration's inquiry into the fight the overseer Mòrag nic Iain Maor bears witness that the pumps were stopped on the agent's order. Her words are struck out. The Lamp-Watch gets a copy of them all the same.

title: The grey fever
body: A fever of the chest comes in on the ships and runs over the whole island, from the capital to the eastern farms. It kills the young and strong more than the old, the Mission notes in alarm. The camps, already hungry, bury more than the towns.

title: The grey fever at Cathair mhòr
body: At Cathair mhòr the grey fever shuts the market for the first time in the town's memory. The custodians' roll gives the dead by street, and the longest list is of the street where the carters lived.

title: The grey fever at Dùn thais
body: At Dùn thais the fever takes the physician the Administration sent to treat it, and two of the Mission's nurses. The old houses of the druid masters are opened as sick-rooms.

title: The second petition
body: This one carries a threat beneath its words, not a plea. It is the first writing of the Dia-thìrich the Administration troubles to answer, and it answers with more guards, not with concessions.

title: The signatories of Cnoc dhìreach
body: Coinneach Ruadh, custodian of Cnoc dhìreach, signs the second petition, and in the same week is turned out of his post as clerk to the Company store. He is one of eleven who sign and lose Company work for it.

title: Eilidh nic Raghnaill
